explanations.answer: So the king won't suffer loss
explanations.explanation: The text says the satraps are accountable to the three administrators “…so that the king would not suffer loss.” Darius, the king over this kingdom, wants somebody keeping an eye on things. With 120 satraps out there, I'd want a few supervisors too. Daniel is one of them.

explanations.answer: So the king can travel freely
explanations.explanation: Packing light is smart for a trip, friend, but travel never comes up in these verses. The reason the text gives is “…so that the king would not suffer loss.” The three administrators are there to keep an eye on the satraps. That's the whole setup.

explanations.answer: So the people can bring complaints
explanations.explanation: I like the thought, but the text doesn't say anything about the people or their complaints. It says the satraps are accountable to the administrators “…so that the king would not suffer loss.” So the point of the arrangement is to protect the king. Daniel is one of the three put in charge of that.

That's it. The king plans to set Daniel over the whole kingdom. That's every satrap, every administrator and everybody else. I can barely supervise one batch, and Daniel is about to get the entire operation.

An army is a big job, but the text doesn't say that. It says the king planned to set Daniel over the whole kingdom. That's a much bigger promotion than one army. Daniel's extraordinary spirit has really made him stand out.

A palace would be a nice corner office, but the king's plan is bigger than that. Verse 3 says he planned to set Daniel over the whole kingdom. That's way past the palace gates. Daniel's extraordinary spirit does that.
They dug hard, but the verse says they could find no charge or corruption. They came up empty. Verse 4 even says that no negligence or corruption was found in him. Not a crumb of it.

Right, they found nothing. The text says they could find no charge or corruption, and that no negligence or corruption was found in him. These men were looking hard and still had nothing to show for it. When you can't find a single crumb on a man's record, that says a lot about him.

That's the reason the text gives. Verse 4 says they found nothing “…because he was trustworthy…” Daniel does his work the same way whether anybody is checking or not. That's a hard record to dig through.

Daniel does stand out in this chapter, but the text doesn't give fame as the reason. It says they came up empty “…because he was trustworthy…” It's his character that left them with nothing to use. Fame doesn't clear anybody's record.

Money isn't mentioned in the verse at all. The reason the text gives is “…because he was trustworthy…” and that's why no negligence or corruption turned up. His honest work is what left them empty-handed.

Yes, that's what they say. They tell each other, “We will never find any charge against this Daniel unless we find something against him concerning the law of his God.” They know his work is spotless. So the one place left to attack is his faith.
His family isn't brought up anywhere in the plan. The men say they need something “…concerning the law of his God.” Nothing else on the list. They are going after how he serves God.

The treasury might sound like a good place to look for trouble, but they already checked the kingdom's business and found nothing (Daniel 6:4). The men say they need something “…concerning the law of his God.” That's their last hope. They are looking at Daniel's faith, not the money.

The decree says anyone who petitions any god or man “except you, O king” will be thrown into the lions' den. They're talking to Darius, so the one exception is Darius himself. Thirty days of everybody asking the king and only the king. I think that decree has someone's pride all over it.

Nebuchadnezzar was a king from earlier in Daniel's book (Daniel 1:18), but he isn't in this decree. The men are speaking to Darius and say, “…except you, O king.” So the exception is the king standing in front of them.

Belshazzar was the king in Daniel 5 (Daniel 5:1), but this decree isn't about him. The men say anyone who petitions any god or man “except you, O king” will be thrown into the lions' den. King Darius is the one they're talking to. He is the exception.

That's right. The men tell Darius to sign it “…so that it cannot be changed—in accordance with the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be repealed.” Once the ink dries, it's done. They had that part planned out carefully.

It actually is true. The men say to sign it so it cannot be changed, in accordance with “…the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be repealed.” So once Darius signs, there's no undoing it. That's what makes this plan so tight.

explanations.answer: He prays just as he had done before
explanations.explanation: Daniel goes into his house and three times a day he gets down on his knees, prays and gives thanks to his God, “…just as he had done before.” The decree didn't change his routine one bit. Some people change plans when the rules do. Daniel isn't one of them.

explanations.answer: He stops praying for thirty days
explanations.explanation: The decree would have made that the safe move, but it isn't what Daniel does. The text says he knelt three times a day, prayed and gave thanks to his God, “…just as he had done before.” Thirty days off his knees didn't happen. His routine stayed the same.

explanations.answer: He prays only in secret at night
explanations.explanation: Hiding would be a sensible plan, but that's not what the text says. Daniel prays in his upper room where the windows open toward Jerusalem. He prays three times a day, “…just as he had done before.” He kept his usual routine, with no night shift added.

Yes, his upper room windows open toward Jerusalem. The text says that's where he kneels, prays and gives thanks. Daniel was one of the exiles from Judah (Daniel 6:13), so I think that view means something to him. That's my guess, though, not the text's.
Persia comes up in the chapter, but not in this verse. The windows of his upper room open toward Jerusalem. That's the direction he faces when he kneels and prays.
Egypt isn't in this story at all. Daniel's upper room has windows that open toward Jerusalem. That's where he gets down on his knees, prays and gives thanks to his God three times a day.
That's the word the text uses. Darius is deeply distressed and sets his mind on delivering Daniel. Whatever the men expected, the king doesn't look pleased with how this is turning out.
That's the opposite of what the text says. Verse 14 tells us the king was deeply distressed and set his mind on delivering Daniel. A man who's relieved doesn't spend the day trying to rescue someone.
Nobody's laughing in this verse, friend. The text says Darius was deeply distressed and set his mind on delivering Daniel. A man who's amused doesn't work until sundown to fix something.
Yes. The text says the king set his mind on delivering Daniel and labored until sundown to rescue him. That's a whole day of effort. Darius isn't just sitting on the throne watching.
It's true. Verse 14 says the king labored until sundown to rescue Daniel. That's a full day of trying to find a way out. The decree was signed, so it didn't get him anywhere, but he tried.

That's what the king says. Right as Daniel is thrown in, Darius tells him, “May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you!” I think that's a king with no more moves left, but that's my guess. Notice he says it about Daniel's God.

explanations.answer: I am sorry it came to this
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't record those words. What Darius says to Daniel is, “May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you!” We do know from verse 14 that he labored until sundown to rescue him. The words themselves are about Daniel's God.

explanations.answer: I will find a way to free you
explanations.explanation: The king had already tried that, all the way until sundown (Daniel 6:14). But the words he says here are different: “May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you!” He's pointing past himself.

That's the word. The king seals the stone with his own signet ring and the rings of his nobles, “…so that nothing concerning Daniel could be changed.” It's a lot of rings for one stone. Nobody was going to sneak in and move that rock.

I get the thought, since a stone does block the view. But the verse gives a different reason. The seal is there “…so that nothing concerning Daniel could be changed.” That's why the king uses his ring and the rings of his nobles.

A big stone might muffle a few sounds, but that's not what the verse says. The text says the king sealed it with his ring and his nobles' rings “…so that nothing concerning Daniel could be changed.” It's all about keeping things exactly as they were.

explanations.answer: If Daniel's God was able to deliver him
explanations.explanation: Yes. In a voice of anguish, the king cries, “O Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to deliver you from the lions?” He calls Daniel a servant of the living God. After a night with no sleep, that's the question he has.

explanations.answer: If Daniel is ready to bow to the king
explanations.explanation: That's not what the king asks. At the den, he cries out in anguish, “O Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to deliver you from the lions?” His question is about Daniel's God.

explanations.answer: If Daniel can forgive him for the decree
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't record a question like that. The king cries out, “O Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to deliver you from the lions?” That's the whole question, and it's about God's power to deliver.

Yes, Daniel says, “My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions.” Daniel doesn't talk about his own courage. He gives the credit to God and the angel He sent. That's a pretty humble report from a man who just spent a night in a lions' den.
Daniel doesn't say that. He says, “My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions.” An angel is the one who goes in, and the lions' mouths are shut.

The king does call Daniel a servant of the living God in verse 20, but that's not who Daniel says shut the lions' mouths. He says, “My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions.” The help came from an angel God sent.

explanations.answer: He was found innocent in God's sight
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Daniel gives. He says, “…for I was found innocent in His sight, and I have done no wrong against you, O king.” He had done nothing to the king, either. The men who accused him had nothing true to say.

explanations.answer: He had fasted and prayed all night
explanations.explanation: The fasting that night was the king's, not Daniel's (Daniel 6:18). Daniel's own reason is, “…for I was found innocent in His sight…” That's the reason he gives for why the lions haven't hurt him.

explanations.answer: He had made an offering to God
explanations.explanation: Daniel never mentions an offering. He says, “…for I was found innocent in His sight, and I have done no wrong against you, O king.” That's the reason he gives for why the lions haven't hurt him.

explanations.answer: He had trusted in his God
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives. When Daniel is lifted out, no wounds whatsoever are found on him, “…because he had trusted in his God.” That's the kind of trust Daniel showed when he kept praying as he always had.

explanations.answer: The king's seal had kept him safe
explanations.explanation: The king did seal the stone, but verse 17 says the seal was there so nothing concerning Daniel could be changed. It was a sealed den full of lions. The text says no wounds were found on Daniel “…because he had trusted in his God.”

explanations.answer: He had stayed awake all night
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say Daniel stayed awake. The one who couldn't sleep was the king (Daniel 6:18). For Daniel, the reason given is that no wounds were found “…because he had trusted in his God.”

Darius says the opposite. About Daniel's God, the king writes, “…He endures forever; His kingdom will never be destroyed, and His dominion will never end.” That's a king declaring that a kingdom bigger than his own has no end. He had just learned that firsthand.

That's right. Darius writes, “…He endures forever; His kingdom will never be destroyed, and His dominion will never end.” So he says God's kingdom won't come to an end. It's a big statement from a man whose own decrees got stuck.

explanations.answer: In the heavens and on the earth
explanations.explanation: That's what Darius writes. He says God “…performs signs and wonders in the heavens and on the earth, for He has rescued Daniel from the power of the lions.” The king's letter reaches every nation and language. He's telling the whole kingdom what happened.

explanations.answer: In the temple and the palace
explanations.explanation: The letter doesn't name the temple or the palace. Darius says God “…performs signs and wonders in the heavens and on the earth…” It's wider than any building.
Those places don't show up in the king's letter. He writes that God “…performs signs and wonders in the heavens and on the earth…” That's everywhere, not just two cities.
